items.title: 30.6 Determining the Possible Structure of a Molecule from 1H NMR

source_refs.note: Topic 30.6 with Example 30.2, as printed (PDF 211). The printed 'No. of peaks = No of protons' and the 3.9 ppm 'doublet' (2-1 = 1) are marked with Book corrections.

blocks.text: The structure of an unknown compound can also be deduced by analyzing its ¹H NMR spectrum. It can be done by putting together the following key pieces of information like a puzzle. To determine the structure:

items: Count the number of peaks in the spectrum. No. of peaks = No of protons
Use the chemical shift of each peak to identify functional groups (use data table).
Use peak area to find the actual number of hydrogen atoms for each peak (this gives the no. of hydrogen atoms present in each environment)
Analyze the splitting pattern and calculate the number of adjacent protons. No. of sub-peaks = n +1; n = No. of sub-peaks – 1
Combine this information to assemble the complete molecular structure.
book_errors: No. of peaks = No of protons

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The number of peaks equals the number of proton environments (sets of equivalent protons), not the number of protons; the peak areas give the number of protons in each environment.

Example 30.2: solution
rows: CH₂- next to an electronegative O atom
H₃C–CO–O–CH₂–CH₃ (the C=O printed with its O above)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The CH₂ next to O has three neighbouring protons (the CH₃ group), so its signal at 3.9 ppm is a quartet, 4 – 1 = 3, as the spectrum shows.
